submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the preposition ' of' when the word immediately before it is a determiner-position quantity word that counts over the complement instead of naming it — a quantifier, numeral, ordinal or wh-selector (one, two, three, four, five, some, many, most, all, both, each, either, neither, none, any, few, several, another, more, other, first, second, third, last, next, which) or a superlative adjective (the largest of, the smallest of, the tallest of reach the line; the worst of, the richest of stay just below) — i.e. the partitive 'quantifier of' construction: 'one of the best', 'most of them', 'the first of the three', 'several of these' all peak at the ' of' token, and in running prose 100% of 'one/some/two/many/several/any/first' + ' of' clear the line while under 1% of the same token after a noun do. It stays at baseline when ' of' is governed by a noun or noun-phrase head (the part of, the number of, the end of, the majority of, a group of, the kind of, hundreds of, dozens of, a lot of, plenty of) or by another preposition, adverb or pronoun (because of, instead of, ahead of, sort of, them of, that of), and it also stays low when the trigger sits at the very start of a text, where there is almost no left context ('Some of the members voted...' in isolation peaks at 0.6, but 'The clerk said some of the members voted...' peaks at 2.6).

rival_explanations: The pole is really a detector of the fixed enumerating phrase 'one of' (with the small number words), which supplies a third of its firings and its highest peaks, so it should fall quiet on 'several of', 'each of' and 'the first of' where no 'one' is present.
The pole fires on ' of' after any expression of quantity, measure nouns included, so it should also fire on 'hundreds of the villagers', 'half of the members' and 'a number of the boxes'.

The pole tracks the determiner slot rather than the partitive construction, so it should fire on ' of' after any closed-class determiner or pronoun ('this of', 'that of', 'them of') and after a determiner followed by any complement preposition ('one from', 'many in').

Finding the right words when children are disappointed isn’t always easy. I’ve learned over the years that although it is hard to see our children feeling upset, distracting, reasoning, lecturing or otherwise trying to fix their feelings usually just backfires. So how do we find the right words to say when children are disappointed? The words that express understanding, empathy, that keep us connected and don’t fix, lecture or distract?
“I believe you” I said to my son the other afternoon.
As my words met his disappointment, I saw his face relax into a small smile. It wasn’t happiness but a smile that showed acceptance and acknowledgement that I had paid attention. I had listened, and although I wasn’t giving into my sons’ request, just three words made it safe for him to feel his disappointment and let it go.
“I really wanted to… I’m, I’m, well, really disappointed.” He offered.
“I believe you.” I had offered in return.
I’d love to say that our exchange was about something profound or delicate, (which in a way it was because all parenting moments seem to be) but not really. We were just dealing with a difference of opinions about taking candy to school. His school doesn’t allow it. My son had thought that putting two pieces of candy in his bag and promising to leave it alone until school was over was a an acceptable way to bend the rules. Being very logical and excellent at keeping his word, I knew that his plan, in his mind, was rock solid. Solid or not, I wasn’t ready to support breaking the school rules and I was setting a limit “I understand your plan and my answer is no.” I had said.
To be completely honest, the rebel in me wanted to let him take the candy, after all, what’s the big deal, it’s two pieces of candy and I knew I could trust him to keep his word. Plus, if he did not keep his word and “got caught” in school, well, that would be his experience to deal with and learn from. The responsible mama in me on the other hand did not want to set a precedent of breaking school rules. I’ll admit that asking critical questions and being willing to break rules for a good cause definitely has it’s time and place, yet, this wasn’t it.
Sometimes, when my son and I disagree we also disconnect. I’ve worked on this over the years, but I still get it wrong at times. In moments like this, he has his ideas and I have mine. My son focuses on his logical solutions and has an enviable talent for living in the moment. I tend to focus far, far ahead into the future, thinking about the “what ifs” and sometimes I let fear take over.
This time, my resolve to not disconnect while setting the limit stuck.
This time I wanted to accept his disappointment for what it was.
This time, I found the right words.
Three simple words in the right moment.

    """Prompt the user to input an integer element."""
    while True:
        try:
            elem = int(input("Enter an integer element to insert: "))
            return elem
        except ValueError:
            print("Invalid input. Please try again.")

def get_position(lst):
    """Prompt the user to input a valid position in the given list."""
    n = len(lst)
    while True:

            if pos < 0 or pos > n:

readings.explanation: The pole fires on the preposition ' of' when the word immediately before it is a determiner-position quantity word that counts over the complement instead of naming it — a quantifier, numeral, ordinal or wh-selector (one, two, three, four, five, some, many, most, all, both, each, either, neither, none, any, few, several, another, more, other, first, second, third, last, next, which) or a superlative adjective (the largest of, the smallest of, the tallest of reach the line; the worst of, the richest of stay just below) — i.e. the partitive 'quantifier of' construction: 'one of the best', 'most of them', 'the first of the three', 'several of these' all peak at the ' of' token, and in running prose 100% of 'one/some/two/many/several/any/first' + ' of' clear the line while under 1% of the same token after a noun do. It stays at baseline when ' of' is governed by a noun or noun-phrase head (the part of, the number of, the end of, the majority of, a group of, the kind of, hundreds of, dozens of, a lot of, plenty of) or by another preposition, adverb or pronoun (because of, instead of, ahead of, sort of, them of, that of), and it also stays low when the trigger sits at the very start of a text, where there is almost no left context ('Some of the members voted...' in isolation peaks at 0.6, but 'The clerk said some of the members voted...' peaks at 2.6).

The pole is really a detector of the fixed enumerating phrase 'one of' (with the small number words), which supplies a third of its firings and its highest peaks, so it should fall quiet on 'several of', 'each of' and 'the first of' where no 'one' is present.
The pole fires on ' of' after any expression of quantity, measure nouns included, so it should also fire on 'hundreds of the villagers', 'half of the members' and 'a number of the boxes'.

The pole tracks the determiner slot rather than the partitive construction, so it should fire on ' of' after any closed-class determiner or pronoun ('this of', 'that of', 'them of') and after a determiner followed by any complement preposition ('one from', 'many in').
